slopdev: is this process already uid 1? read it on both ends of the sandwich

The retry fallback earned its keep -- the fd number was taken even inside one
chain, and it recovered:

    NETCTRL-SANDWICH  close=0-setuid=0-socket=124-setuid2=0-wanted=122
    NETCTRL-UAF-RETRY wanted=122-strays=124-landedOn=122
    NETCTRL-UAF       uaf_sock=122-reusedFdNumber=YES

But there is a pattern across every run in this session that I should have
seen sooner: a CLEAR that returns 0 has NEVER been followed by a completed
race. Not once. The attempt whose CLEAR returned -1 ran the flush, the crfree
and the twin scan and reported a row; every attempt whose CLEAR returned 0 is
the last thing in its transcript. That was true two commits before ttyMark
existed, so it is not the logging -- it is the over-release.

The two setuid(1) calls exist so that each hands the thread a NEW ucred, and
the credential CLEAR frees is one the thread is no longer running on. If this
WebProcess is ALREADY uid 1, setuid(1) is a no-op, no new cred is allocated,
and CLEAR frees the credential under the running thread -- and the next syscall
that touches a cred walks freed memory. That is precisely the observed
behaviour, and the sandwich's own returns cannot tell it apart from success:
setuid returns 0 either way.

So read getuid() on both ends of the sandwich, inside the pre-free window where
syscalls cost nothing:

    NETCTRL-SANDWICH uidBefore=N-close=0-setuid=0-socket=..-setuid2=0-uidAfter=N

uidBefore == 1 would explain every successful CLEAR killing the process, and
would mean the trigger needs a different way to get a fresh credential on this
console.

Also promote NETCTRL-CLEAR-PRE to the serial channel. NETCTRL-CLEAR itself is
deliberately off it now, so without this there is nothing to distinguish "died
issuing the CLEAR" from "died somewhere after it" -- and the pre side is safe.

slopdev: no syscalls between the over-release and the reclaim

    [slopkit 13] NETCTRL-UAF   uaf_sock=113-reusedFdNumber=YES
    [slopkit 14] NETCTRL-CLEAR ret=0-ok
    <crash>

CLEAR returning 0 IS the over-release. From the instant it returns, the
credential this process runs on may be freed while td_ucred still points at it,
and the next syscall that touches a cred walks freed memory. Dying there is
what a working over-release looks like -- and it is also what an unnecessary
syscall after one looks like, because ttyMark() is a chain launch and I had put
one immediately after the CLEAR to log its return.

Both readings fit the same transcript, which is reason enough to stop paying
for the second while trying to observe the first. NETCTRL-CLEAR goes back to
flushMark: still on the screen, still in the durable trail, no syscall. The
clearRet is carried out through the attempt report to STAGE0-ROW instead --
raised after the attempt is over, on the serial channel, where it costs
nothing:

    STAGE0-ROW a1-s4-find-twins-...-uaf=113/Y/0-95ms

That window is the whole exploit. It should contain the flush, the crfree and
the spray, and nothing else -- certainly not logging.

slopdev: name the race step in the trail -- the sandwich now works

The trigger finally executed correctly, end to end:

    [slopkit 11] NETCTRL-SET      slot=-1-ret=0-ok
    [slopkit 12] NETCTRL-SANDWICH close=0-setuid=0-socket=113-setuid2=0-wanted=113
    [slopkit 13] NETCTRL-UAF      uaf_sock=113-reusedFdNumber=YES-closeRet=0-setuidCalls=2
    [slopkit 14] NETCTRL-CLEAR    ret=0-ok

All four syscalls in one chain returned cleanly, the fresh socket landed on the
exact number the discard socket had, and CLEAR matched the slot and returned 0
-- so the over-release happened. That is the first time the primitive has been
performed as designed on this console.

And then the transcript ends. What follows CLEAR is the race: the iov flush,
the post-flush crfree, the twin scan. None of it is on the serial channel, and
it should NOT be -- a chain round trip per step inside a 27ms race window is
exactly the kind of instrumentation that changes what it is measuring.

It does not need to be. Every RACE-STEP already reaches the durable trail; it
was just being recorded as a bare "RACE-STEP", twelve times, which says only
that the race was running. Fold the step name in -- s0-free-all-rthdrs,
s2-iov-flush-32, s4-find-twins -- and the trail narrates the whole race for
free, because the write happens either way. Not one syscall added to the
window.

So a death in there is now named on the next load, by the auto-run gate that is
already there to catch it:

    POOPS-AUTORUN-REFUSED prevDiedAt=RACE-STEP:s3-post-flush-crfree

slopdev: remember which slot and which fd a dead run left behind

Same boot as the last transcript, eight minutes later, and both slots gone --
one of them leaked by the run the emit() bug killed after it had already armed
slot 0. A crash between SET_QUEUE and CLEAR_QUEUE costs a slot permanently, and
there are two a boot.

The interesting part is that those slots are SYSTEM-WIDE. "consumed by an
earlier trigger this boot" survives the WebProcess dying and respawning, so the
table outlives the process that filled it. And CLEAR_QUEUE matches a slot by
the fd NUMBER stored in it -- a number interpreted in whatever process asks
now, not in the one that armed it. So a slot left behind by a dead run still
names an fd, and that number is the entire input a later run would need to hand
it back.

Start recording it: TRIGGER-ARMED already says "took slot 0 on fd 122", so
parse the slot and the fd out of it and keep them next to the pid in the spent
record. Nothing reads it yet -- this is one localStorage write on a mark that
fires twice a boot, and the prerequisite for doing anything about a leaked slot
later.

slopdev: emit() must not fcall a by-number-only syscall -- SETUID is one

Fresh boot, slots free, and the transcript stops dead:

    [slopkit 10] TEST ps1_prepare-PASS-why=80 IPv6 sockets in the 0x168 class...
    [slopkit 11] NETCTRL-SET slot=-1-ret=0-ok
    <nothing>

Between NETCTRL-SET and NETCTRL-UAF there is exactly one new thing: the
close/setuid/socket/setuid sandwich that 29c68eb put into a single chain to
stop the fd number being lost. It uses emit(), and emit() did

    chain.fcall(P.syscalls[num], ...)

i.e. it jumps to the stub ADDRESS. On this console main.js reports

    SYSCALL-BYNUMBER 35 stub(s) with an unknown address are callable by
                     number | 0x17=by number

and gives each of those an entry pointing at the bare syscall instruction --
correct for fsyscall, which loads rax first, and catastrophic for a raw fcall,
which executes whatever number rax happened to hold. 0x17 is SETUID. Two of
the four slots in that sandwich were wild syscalls.

The old code was safe by accident: it called sys() four separate times, and
sys() goes through the by-number path. Batching them was right for the fd
window and wrong about how emit() invokes.

Fixed in emit() rather than at the call site, because every other emit() in the
engine has the same trap waiting: hand by-number-only syscalls to fsyscall(),
which already picks correctly between a proven address, a missing syscall
instruction, and a number. Nothing else changes -- syscalls with a real address
still go straight to it.

Added NETCTRL-SANDWICH carrying all four returns, so the next time this line is
the last one it says which of the four failed.

slopdev: I broke the console channel one commit after proving it

ad934c6 rebuilt tty() around runBuilt/emit/retPtr to get all three candidate
channels into a single chain. retPtr() and armRet() read S.buf -- and the FIRST
tty call is PS1-ENTER, which ps1_prepare raises before it reaches
buildBuffers(). S.buf is still null there, so the very first line threw and the
channel was gone for the whole run, one commit after it had been shown working.

Back to sys(), which carries its own return cell and depends on nothing. 0x259
stays first because it is the proven one; fd 1 and fd 2 remain per-call
fallbacks rather than a one-shot probe, so a single refusal cannot pin the
channel to "none" for the rest of the run.

The three-way-probe-in-one-chain idea was not worth what it cost: the thing it
was buying -- not trusting a single syscall return as proof of visibility --
was already answered the moment the lines appeared in the serial log.

The pin still comes from a three-way probe in one chain rather than from any
single return, because a syscall returning success is not by itself evidence
its output is visible anywhere -- which is exactly the mistake that made the
first attempt look like a dead end.

    TWIN-SCAN-DONE     TEST <row>-<status>-why=...

The per-row TEST line goes out from the ladder runner, between rows, which is a
safe place to spend a chain round trip -- guarded on the engine existing and
the chain being alive, and wrapped, so logging can never be what kills a run.

slopdev: the auto-run gate was arming itself

    PREV-TRAIL died-after=POOPS-AUTORUN-REFUSED<PREV-TRAIL-steps=2
    POOPS-AUTORUN-REFUSED prevDiedAt=POOPS-AUTORUN-REFUSED-steps=2

My fault, and obvious in hindsight: the refusal emits marks of its own, marks
go into the trail through screenMark like every other mark, and the next load
then sees a non-empty trail with no POOPS-COMPLETE in it -- which is the exact
condition to refuse. Two loads in and the page could never run again.

Two changes, either of which alone would fix it, and both are worth having:
the decision ignores the gate's own bookkeeping tags, and the trail is wiped on
the way out of the gate whether it refused or not. So a trail of nothing but
refusal marks is not a death, and a refusal cannot leave anything behind for
the next load to trip over.

slopdev: an auto-reload after a crash must not spend the boot

The exhausted verdict now reads correctly:

    POOPS-VERDICT REBOOT-triggered=0-...-reasons=1
    POOPS-VERDICT-WHY both netcontrol slots were already spent earlier this boot
    reboot required -- 2 PASS / 2 FAIL

but that is the third boot running where the slots were gone before anyone got
to look at it, and the cause is in the first crash.txt: when the WebProcess
dies the browser respawns and reloads this page by itself, 4 to 13 seconds
later, same URL. This page auto-runs. So the first run of a boot is regularly
an unattended one nobody sees, it arms and spends both slots, and every load
after it can only say "already spent earlier this boot".

The trail is exactly the signal for this and nothing else was: non-empty, so a
previous load in this browser session got somewhere, and no POOPS-COMPLETE in
it, so that load never finished. entry() now stops there, names where the last
load died, and offers a reload. The trail is consumed on the way in, so the
operator's own reload runs normally -- one refusal, not a lock-out.

That turns the post-crash reload from the thing that quietly costs a boot into
the thing that reports the crash.

slopdev: log to the devkit console -- sceKernelDebugOutText is syscall 0x259

Your idea, and the NID does exist. libkernel_web on this build exports

    sceKernelDebugOutText   9JYNqN6jAKI#I#A   rva 0x00AE00

and the function is three instructions:

    push rbp ; mov rbp,rsp
    mov  rdx, rdi        ; the caller's channel
    mov  edi, 7
    call 0x36880         ; mov rax,0x259 ; mov r10,rcx ; syscall
    pop  rbp ; ret

So the chain does not need the module at all -- it raises syscall 0x259 BY
NUMBER, which also side-steps this console's build shift, and
syscall_map[0x259] = 0x00036880 is already in offsets/7.00.js. Args exactly as
the wrapper passes them: (7, text, channel).

This is the only log channel a WebProcess death cannot erase. Everything else
lives inside the dying process: the screen repaints at most every 250ms inside
a race window, queued marks go with the heap, and the localStorage trail
survives but is only readable on the NEXT load. Text handed to 0x259 is in the
kernel's hands the moment the syscall returns, and Target Manager already has
it -- in order, with nothing dropped.

E.tty(text) and E.ttyMark(tag, extra) added. Deliberately NOT wired into
flushMark: tty launches a ROP chain, the chain is a single shared resource, and
firing one from an unawaited mark handler would interleave it with whatever
chain is already running. Every call site awaits, and the sites are the ones
whose output has actually been lost:

    PS1-ENTER PS1-RTPRIO PS1-PINNED PS1-BUFFERS PS1-SOCKETPAIRS
    PS1-PIPES PS1-GROUPS PS1-SPAWNED
    NETCTRL-SET NETCTRL-UAF NETCTRL-CLEAR
    STAGE0-ROW STAGE0-STEPS

The first call reports the syscall's return once as a TTY mark, so the screen
says whether the channel works before anyone goes looking for it. Lines are
tagged "[slopkit N] " with a sequence number, so a gap in the console output is
visible as a gap.

slopdev: a run that could not arm must end saying REBOOT, not FAILED

ps1_prepare passed and the PS1-* marks painted, so the repaint fix works. The
run then did nothing at all:

    NETCTRL-SET slot=-1-ret=-1, errno set but not readable from here
    NETCTRL-SET slot=1 -ret=-1, errno set but not readable from here
    TRIGGER-EXHAUSTED both netcontrol slots were consumed by an earlier trigger
    POOPS-VERDICT FINE-triggered=0-alias=0-...-reasons=0
    FAILED -- 3 PASS / 1 FAIL

"FAILED" is the wrong word for it and it is the last line on the screen, which
is the one line always in frame. verdict() collects reasons for a reboot from
things the run DID -- the trigger fired, setuid was called, an alias exists --
and an exhausted run does none of them, so reasons=0, reboot=false, and the
banner falls through to a generic failure while the only remedy is a power
cycle. An earlier run with the same cause said "reboot required" only because
it had managed to arm once first.

Record the exhaustion in S.slotsExhausted where attemptRace already detects it,
and add it to verdict() LAST, so it can never displace a reason describing
something the run actually did. It is the only reason that can fire on a run
which changed nothing.

slopdev: make ps1's steps survive their own death

Another ps1 crash, and this time not one PS1-* mark on screen. That is not
evidence the death was before PS1-RTPRIO: ps1_prepare runs entirely inside
setRaceMode(true), and inside a race window screenLine repaints at most every
250ms (SCREEN_MS). Everything logged in the quarter-second before the process
dies never reaches the DOM. The seven marks added for exactly this span are the
one thing guaranteed to be lost in it.

Two fixes, both narrow:

  - screenMark forces repaintScreen() for PS1-* tags only. Seven marks, once
    each per run, so the throttle keeps doing its job everywhere else.
  - PREV-TRAIL is printed twice: at the top of main(), and again immediately
    above "running the ladder". The console holds 500 lines and auto-scrolls,
    so anything said at the top of a run is long gone by the time the run dies
    -- and the trail is only ever read AFTER a death. Above the ladder it sits
    a few lines from ps0/ps1, which is the part of the screen that gets
    photographed.

The trail itself is already correct for this: since REV 60 it is taken in
screenMark, so race-window marks reach it even though flushMark defers them.

slopdev: the fd number was being lost between close() and socket()

The trigger's own returns, visible for the first time:

    attempt 1  NETCTRL-UAF   uaf_sock=124-reusedFdNumber=NO-122
               NETCTRL-CLEAR ret=-1
    attempt 2  NETCTRL-UAF-RECYCLED closed=124-before-new-sandwich
               NETCTRL-UAF   uaf_sock=122-reusedFdNumber=YES-setuidCalls=4
               NETCTRL-CLEAR ret=0-ok

That is the whole failure, and it is exactly what the kernel predicted. 7.00's
CLEAR_QUEUE matches a queue slot by the FD NUMBER stored at slot+0x10
(`mov edx,[rdi+0x10] ; cmp edx,[r14]`), so everything depends on the fresh
socket landing on the number the discard socket had. Attempt 1 closed 122 and
got 124 back, so CLEAR matched no slot, returned -1, and spent one of the two
netcontrol slots this boot has for nothing. Attempt 2 -- which only got its
number because the previous attempt's stray 124 had just been recycled -- did
land on 122 and CLEAR returned 0.

The window was four separate chain launches wide: close, setuid, socket, setuid
with JS and awaits between each, milliseconds during which any other thread in
this WebProcess that opens a descriptor takes the number first. Put all four in
ONE chain and the window is four syscalls long.

Plus a fallback for the case a chain cannot prevent -- the number already gone
before the close. Hold each wrong descriptor so the allocator cannot hand it
straight back, yield, ask again, up to four times, then return every stray.
Reported as NETCTRL-UAF-RETRY with what it wanted and where it landed.

Worth two attempts a boot instead of one, and the twin scan finally gets a run
where the sandwich actually completed. poops.js v=77.

slopdev: offsets/7.00.js does not parse -- seven duplicate consts

"can't find variable wk_gadgetmap" is not a missing variable. fd2a9e6 appended
a kernel-offsets block to the end of offsets/7.00.js that re-declares seven
names already declared at lines 553-565:

    OFFSET_KERNEL_ALLPROC, _DATA, _ROOTVNODE,
    _QA_FLAGS, _SECURITY_FLAGS, _TARGETID, _UTOKEN_FLAGS

A duplicate `const` is a SyntaxError for the WHOLE file, so nothing in it is
declared -- not the kernel offsets, not wk_gadgetmap, not syscall_map, not one
gadget. `node --check offsets/7.00.js` says so in one line; the other fifteen
profiles all pass.

Why it surfaced so far from the cause: window.offsetsReady resolves on the
script element's LOAD event, and a script that fails to PARSE still fires load.
So the run sails past the "offsets script was never injected" and "offsets 404"
checks and dies on the first symbol it touches.

The appended block wins -- it is identical for ALLPROC/DATA/ROOTVNODE and it
actually derives the four Sony flag words the old block left at 0 (QA_FLAGS
0x01718088, SECURITY_FLAGS 0x01718064, TARGETID 0x0171806D, UTOKEN_FLAGS
0x017180F0). The seven old declarations are removed, their provenance comments
moved down to the values they describe, and the three genuinely unique ones
(STACK_COOKIE, STACK_SYS_SCHED_YIELD_RET, SYS_SCHED_YIELD_RET) stay put.

Sanity-checked against the memory of the derivation: ALLPROC 0x034A9D50 minus
OFFSET_KERNEL_DATA 0xC50000 is kdata+0x2859D50, and ROOTVNODE 0x03D17510 minus
the same is kdata+0x30C7510 -- both the values found in procinit() and VFS_ROOT.

preflight() now asks for wk_gadgetmap and syscall_map behind a try/catch and
reports "reported load but did NOT evaluate", naming the profile and its src,
so the next syntax error says what it is instead of pointing at a variable.

slopdev: show the netcontrol trigger's own returns -- the bug IS on 7.00

The census came back perfect and empty:

    TWIN-FIRST-CALLS set_rthdr[0]=0-get_rthdr[0]=0-optlen[0]=8-tag[0]=0x13370000-sprayLen=360
    TWIN-SCAN-DONE reason=budget-a=10-ms=31-spray=0-read=0-self=800/800-untch=0-notag=0-optlen=0

800 of 800 sockets read back their OWN tag. No spray failed, no read failed,
nothing was untouched, no optlen was wrong. The spray works perfectly and
nothing ever aliases, so the chunk is never handed out twice.

Two things checked against 700_dvk_kernel.elf, both settled:

1. UCRED_SIZE 0x168 is CORRECT for 7.00, so the spray is in the right zone.
   crget is `mov edi, 0x168 ; lea rsi, [M_CRED] ; mov edx, 0x102 ; call malloc`
   at ffffffff804f8580, and a second crget-shaped site at ffffffff804fa740
   agrees. M_CRED at ffffffff8195ffb0, identified by ks_magic 0x3454f8e9 with
   ks_shortdesc -> "cred". cr_groups is at +0x118 and cr_smallgroups at +0x124,
